speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There must be some final court of appeal for decision in these questions of salary. Parliament has assigned to the Civil Service Commission the duty, amongst other things, of determining the salaries to be paid to civil servants. The government, in order to ensure the fairest possible consideration for civil servants in that connection, required that the Civil Ser-virs Commission should prepare its report in conjunction with the deputy ministers, and also in conjunction with the Audit Board. The government has taken particular care to see that the commission should carry out its wishes in that regard, and has on two or three different occasions referred back the report submitted by the commission to the government, before its final acceptance. I may mention that on the first or second occasion on which the Civil Service Commission submitted its report the report was signed by two of the commissioners. The postal employees requested that if possible the government obtain the signature of all three commissioners before accepting any report from them. The government insisted on that additional step, and the position of matters now is that the report has been made. The government had either to approve it or disapprove it. To disapprove it was to leave the salaries where they were; to approve it was to give effect to such increases as had been made by the Civil Service Commission. Unless parliament is prepared to revise the act which refers these matters to the Civil Service Commission and transfer the authority to some other source, I do not see that it is possible for the government to consider the report further. It would simply mean sending it back to the commissioners who would return it with the statement that that was their final judgment. I may add that they have set out at considerable length, in the statement accompanying the report, the reasons which have actuated them. The Audit Board has also placed its views on record. All these different views have been presented to the House in the papers which I have laid on the Table.

I do
not find among the papers that were laid on the Table the correspondence exchanged between the Post Office Department and the Civil Service Commission. Will the government lay that on the Table?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to
direct the attention of the House to a despatch appearing in the morning papers from Vancouver containing a statement made by one of the papers in that city with reference to the forthcoming arrival of the British special service squadron on June 21. The Vancouver paper states that there will be no member of the Dominion government to welcome the ships, and it goes on to say that despatches from Ottawa indicate that members of the cabinet are too busy in the House to come to British Columbia, and that the British Columbia people are not quite satisfied with the situation. It goes on to say:
They recall that when the fleet was at South African ports Premier Smuts extended the welcome. In Australia Premier Bruce met them, and Premier Massey extended a welcome at New Zealand.
It goes on to say that Ottawa has shown little interest in the visit of the fleet, and it continues:
Its grant toward entertainment has disappointed Victoria and Vancouver, and there is a growing feeling that the Dominion authorities are conserving their energies in this respect until the warships reach Halifax and Quebec in August.
I desire to say that this statement is a very unfair one. The attitude of the government toward the cruise of this squadron and its visit to our Canadian ports is one of the friendliest interest, and we are animated only by the desire to extend the fullest and most appreciative welcome to those representative ships of His Majesty's navy. Our friends in British Columbia are hardly right in their reference to the visit of the squadron to Australia. The visit to Australia took place in March last, and the ships first called at the port of Freemantle, where they were received by the Governor of the state, and it was not until they had practically made the round of the island of Australia and came to Melbourne that Premier Bruce welcomed them there officially on behalf of that Dominion, Melbourne being the capital of the state. What we have done in regard to extending a welcome to the squadron has been that on behalf of the government, the officers of the squadron will be entertained on their arrival on the Pacific coast at a formal dinner, and in conjunction with the government of Alberta we have arranged to take twenty-five officers and two hundred and fifty of other ratings on these vessels through to Edmonton, visiting intermediate points, and from Edmonton to Calgary, and then back to Vancouver. We have asked the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia to officially welcome the officers of the squadron to Canada on our behalf, and to preside at the official dinner which is to be given them on their arrival.
The squadron also expects to visit Halifax and Quebec, and I am sure that our friends in British Columbia can feel that there is no desire to discriminate, and there will be no discrimination, in regard to the expenditure of money as between the eastern ports and that great city on the Pacific coast.
As to the question of the right hon. the Prime Minister going out at this time to officially welcome the squadron, I am sure it is the judgment of the House, and that it would be in the judgment of the country, that it can hardly be expected that the House could spare the presence of its leader at this time, no matter how keen he may be to show the greatest possible attention to the officers of the squadron. For a similar reason I think the House will feel that this duty, which might otherwise fall upon me, would be rather difficult to perform at this time, having regard to the important matters before the House. We are looking forward, however, to having the representatives of the officers of the squadron visit the capital of

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
There has been a reduction in this
vote of $5,000. The amount is required to make provision for repairs and improvements to harbour and river works under the control of the Department of Public Works in the province of Manitoba. It is the regular vote.

Where is the money to be
spent?

It is to be spent
on the care of the harbour and river works under the control of the Department of Public Works.
On the Red river?

On various rivers.
Last year there were expenditures on the Pas river, the Red river, and Victoria beach.

Item agreed to.
Portage la Prairie-sewer extension, $23,000.

I think I shall
give a review of what led up to this expenditure. The matter was discussed very fully in the House last year. In the year 1908 a petition to the Dominion government from a number of people living in the vicinity of Portage la Prairie suggested that the river would be relieved during the time of the spring freshet by the digging of a cut or canal which would straighten the river at that point. The work was undertaken and carried on, and each year during the flooded time it served a useful purpose until 1921 or 1922. The cut then widened to such an extent that it left the bed of the old channel dry, and in that way exposed the sewer outlet of the city of Portage la Prairie. The city complained very bitterly to the department of this condition, which had arisen, as they claimed, from the activities of the department, and last year we brought in a vote for the work. A good deal of correspondence and negotiation took place with the city in order to bring about a condition that would be satisfactory to the citizens. Finally tenders were

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
called for and three bids were received, the prices varying from $76,300 to $99,219. These tenders were above the estimate prepared by the departmental engineer whose estimate was $60,000 odd. We rather hesitated to let the contract on account of the variation between the estimate of the departmental engineer and the contractors' tenders. However, it was claimed that owing to the nature of the soil in that district it was very difficult to ascertain what would be encountered after getting below the surface Experience had shown the contractors that in this deep trenching there was a probability of caving in and great uncertainty, as to what might happen. However, we let a contract in December of last year for the work. It has been proceeded with, and I believe the sewer is satisfactorily installed. Just at this point I wish to state that the fears of the contractor were somewhat realized, because after he had dug this trench. three feet wide, which was the intended development, he found that he had to put in cribbing. This made it impossible for him to place his eighteen-inch sewer pipe and be able to caulk the joints. The result was that he had to move another foot of dirt on one side of the trench for its entire length. I mention this because the contractor has made a claim upon the department for this extra work. The matter is under consideration, and the district engineer has advised that the department should give the contractor consideration as to the actual cost. The committee will be advised if the matter comes up in the supplementary estimates.

What was the
amount of the tender that was accepted?
What was the estimate of the departmental engineer?

Did the minister not
tell us that the tender exceeded the estimate of the departmental engineer because of the uncertain conditions which the contractor expected to encounter? And is it not fair to suppose that his tender was high enough to cover the conditions which he feared might be met with?

He claims not.
He figured he would get through with a three-foot trench, but such an amount of cribbing was required that he had to enlarge his trench to four feet. The vote we are asking for is to cover the present contract.
Without any extras?
Without any extras.

Has this work
been done to the satisfaction of the town, and will it prevent the flooding that has caused so much damage in the past?

This work was
done to take care of the sewerage outlet of the city, so that the outlet will be protected We have not done anything to the river itself under this expense.

I have a lively recollection of what was said by my leadei (Mr. Meighen) in the House last year on this subject. I am under the impression his lhought was that the department was going to relieve the district from the direct results of departmental work. Now, I understand this work is merely to look after the sewer, and not to provide against the flooding at all.
We have tried to accomplish what the city desired and I believe the work has been done to its satisfaction.

I may say that I have
heard no complaints, although there may be some which have not come to my attention.

I think the work
is satisfactory to the city.

I believe the work is satisfactory to the city of Portage la Prairie, at any rate there has been a statement in the newspapers to that effect: I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister and the government upon taking hold of the situation and putting it back to where it was in 1908. What I mean by that is this:	The
department diverted the water of the river by digging a canal in 1908. Through the subsequent years up to 1922 there was a gradual wearing away of the cut thus creating a. bigger canal. Finally it took the whole course of the river, thereby leaving bare the mouth of the sewer of the city of Portage la Prairie. This created a very disagreeable and very menacing situation and overtures were made to the government on the subject. I am glad to be able to say that the department took hold of the situation and put it back to where they found it in 1908. I believe the citizens of Portage la Prairie duly appreciate the fact and I think I can convey their thanks to the government for their prompt action.
Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Do you think the work has been economically carried out?
The situation was very unpleasant. It had to be taken care of. Whether the work was economically carried out or not I cannot say, but I believe it is satisfactory.

Speaking generally, and
not with any particular reference to this work, does the minister think it is sound business to give such favourable consideration to claims for extra remuneration because of unforeseen circumstances, such as have been referred to in this case? It seems to me it works an injustice to others. What happens in a case like this? Tenders are called for, and one firm puts in a bid that they look upon as final. If their hopes are realized they make a profit, and if not they lose. Another firm puts in a tender a little bit lower and secures the contract, with the intention of making a further claim later on. I am afraid that is often done and I do not think it is wise or fair. If a firm find they have made considerable money, and these unforeseen difficulties did not turn up, they do not refund anything to the public treasury.

These things come up in regard to the contracts from time to time. I have not made up my mind as to what shall be done in this matter. Representations have been made by the engineering department. I would not suggest that the government go further than the actual mst of this unforeseen work. That is a matter to be discussed when they ask for a further amount later on. Each contract and all the conditions must be considered on their merits. In this case there was a great variation in the tenders, ranging from $70,000 to $99,000,-indicating that in the minds of the contractors there was an unforseen quantity there that was very difficult to judge.

This contractor expected
to take out a three-foot trench and he found he had to take out a four-foot trench. Will the engineers of the department say that the extra foot was necessary? Or was it just a little bit of a job he added?
No, it was necessary.

What is the
name of the contractors?
Fowler, Young & Co., Winnipeg.

Item agreed to.
Victoria Beach-wharf repairs, $4,500.
Is that a public wharf?

This item is for
the following work:
To renew the stringers and decking, also to cut off the top portion of closely driven round pilles-about four or five feet, now rotten and falling to pieces- and replace same with timbers laid longitudinally.

I understood there was some embankment made on the Assiniboine river to

prevent flooding. Has anything been done in that respect?

Between what
points?

Between Winnipeg and Portage la Prairie. I understood surveys were to be made of the river and some report made as to whether anything could be done to prevent flooding. A tremendous amount of damage is done every year by the Assini-boine overflowing its banks and destroying highway grades and flooding lands. I have never seen any reports in connection with that matter.

Surveys have been made and the matter is still being developed in the engineering department. The work involves a very considerable sum of money, and we are not bringing down any estimate for it this j^ear.

Fortunately the water was
very low this year and there were no complaints; if the water had been high as usual, there would have been a tremendous amount of damage. As soon as one flood passes over people forget about it until we have another flood.

Fortunately the
floods do not come every year.
They come pretty frequently.

Item agreed to.
Fort Resolution-wharf, $5,120.
Mr! KNOX:	I call the minister's attention
to the fact that some improvements are required on the river leading from Montreal lake out into lake Laronge, which is an extension of the Churchill river. This is a highway leading into the north. A wagon road has been constructed from Prince Albert to Montreal lake, largely by the provincial government; but, although boats are passing through regularly on the river I spoke of, there, are some obstructions between Montreal lake and lake Laronge, which impede progress very much, and I have been informed it would not require a very large amount of money to remove the obstructions which are in the form of boulders in the river. If this were done the outlet into the north country would be very much improved. Will the minister have this matter looked into and brought to the attention of the department?

Yes, I shall be
glad to do so.
Has the minister an appropriation in this amount to take care of the damage at High river.

There is no special appropriation for that. My hon. friend has made representations regarding certain river banks where work should be done; the department has had reports; and negotiations have been proceeding between the munioi-palitiy and individuals interested, the department at Ottawa and the provincial government. I think there has been a suggested authorization, on condition of joint expenditures by the municipalities and the province.

I understand that the department was willing to expend $2,500 if the municipality and private owners would take care of the balance. I see from a communication in the High River Times that the town authorities think that the amount which was at first estimated as being necessary to cover the cost of the required work might not be nearly sufficient, and they are reluctant to embark on the work until they can have some assurance that this amount would be large enough. I should like, if possible, to have the assurance of the minister that his engineer would visit High river again as soon as possible, and that whatever amount is necessary to take care of the share which the Dominion government is willing to assume will be provided, should that be possible.

While discussing this item and the reference my hon. friend has made to expenditures at High river, I might explain to the committee the attitude of the government, or the Department of Public Works, in regard to works of this character. There is no legislative authority as to the manner of control of these rivers. The practice followed from time to time in the past where representations have been made by members of parliament, boards of trade, municipalities or provinces, for expenditures, has been to deal with each case more or less as an individual case. We are rather taking the position that in the case of river bank protection, the people who have located on the river bank, who have property there, are the people primarily interested in saving their property. If the project is beyond them and they are in a municipality, we feel that this becomes primarily the duty of the municipality. If it is beyond the municipality and a public interest is involved, we feel that the provincial government should interest themselves. If it is found that the matter is beyond the individual, the municipality and the provincial government, and that there is

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
a Dominion interest, I think the department and the government are willing to consider each case on its merits. It is only fair, however, to say that these expenditures are asked for from time to time, oftentimes without much consideration as to the cost and the effect the work may have on the river generally. This matter which we discussed just a few moments ago was entered into on a petition in 1908, and it resulted in parliament this year being asked for a vote. I am satisfied that if the municipality of Portage la Prairie had been a party to that arrangement and the matter had been done along proper lines, there would have been a different story to tell to-day and we would not be voting this money. We are being asked, from time to time, through not only the prairie country but the whole of Canada, to come to the relief of individuals, municipalities and cities by way of expenditures on river-bank protection. If we could lay down a principle such as I suggest, many of these cases would not come to government or to parliament and expenditures would not be asked for. I am satisfied, if that principle was laid down and followed, a request of that kind would be jointly examined and reported upon, and I believe the result would probably be better than it has been in the past. In the prairie provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, where the Dominion government control the natural resources and the land, the case is different sometimes from that in eastern Canada and in British Columbia, outside of the railway belt where the river bank and the bed of the river are owned by the province. At the present time in the Northwest Territories and the railway belt the Dominion government still owns the river banks and river bed. I thought I would just make this statement so as to make clear, if possible, the line that the department is following as regards matters of this kind.

What does the minister mean by the "bed" of a river? Does he mean that the alveus of the stream belongs to the province, or does he refer to some navigable stream? I can understand, in the case of navigable rivers, if repairs are needed, the Dominion might have an interest, but I do not understand why the Dominion should be called upon to repair erosions of banks of streams merely for the purpose of protecting private property. Such a thing would be unheard of in New Brunswick. In the St. John river, for instance, the individual is largely responsible for the care of his own bank unless there is a highway along the bank, in which case the province takes care of the matter. I have never before heard of the I Mr. J. H. King.]
Dominion being expected or asked to take care of a situation of that kind, and it will be news to the people in the East that that has been done.
It has been done.
Both the Red river and the Assiniboine river are navigable streams theoretically. As a matter of fact they are not, but they are considered to be, navigable streams.
They have a very large quantity of water in them at certain seasons of the year and they become very dangerous.

Highwood river, that is down the river in this municipality, is navigable in certain parts; but at the point where the damage has been done it is not navigable. At the same time I think the municipality is quite justified in asking this government for some assistance. The Dominion government own the water in all the streams in Alberta; they own all the natural resources; they own the land along the banks of those streams. The provincial government never had any jurisdiction over either the water in the streams or the land alongside of them. If the damage is more than the property owners and the municipality can take care of, if any government is to assist those people, it should be, I say, the Dominion government. I do not think this is the first occasion upon which the federal government has been asked for help in such cases or the first occasion that they have given help. Highwood river is a mountain stream and it is subject to very sudden freshets in the spring of the year when the snow on the mountain melts. One year ago the flood was very much worse because we had about two weeks' heavy rain at a time when we usually get high water. The town of High River was flooded. The main street, I think, was under two or three feet of water for days at a time. The river threatened to break through and change its course, in which case probably most of the water would have gone down the Little Bow river. The Irrigation department of the federal government did some work along the banks of Highwood river to prevent the river from changing its course. They did this, I understand, because the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have water rights on Highwood river for irrigation purposes, and if this water were diverted to the Little Bow river the Canadian Pacific irrigation district would go short of water. If the water had been allowed to take its course and go down Little Bow river, it is quite possible the town, of

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
High River would not have been in danger in any way. Therefore, I think there is no doubt that the Dominion government has some responsibility, and the Minister of Public Works has taken a fair attitude in regard to the work at High river.
Many public works entered into in Canada should be entered into on the basis which the minister has suggested. If municipalities in many cases where they want post offices built were required to put up forty or fifty per cent of the cost of the building, the Department of Public Works, I am sure, would not be called upon to erect so many post offices.

Does the hon. member
think that the cases are comparable? The post oflice in a community such as the one 1 represent is a money-making proposition for the government; a much larger revenue is taken in than the cost involved in running it or the capital expenditure incurred in the building itself. The two things are not comparable.

I might tell the hon
gentleman too that in my own town we have paid in the last ten years over $1,000,000 to the treasury although we have not a public building.
That is right.

The town of High River
I have no doubt has contributed a good many dollars to the revenue of the country; I am not saying anything about that. I know, however, that some work has been done under the vote for harbours and rivers in Ontario which would never have been done if the municipalities had been required to bear any percentage of the cost. But I do not wish to dwell on that feature; we could bring before the committee a good many cases in which money could have been saved to the department in this way. But I do ask the committee to take a fair view of the situation in regard to those towns that are exposed to damage from floods. I want to bring to the attention of the minister the circumstances in connection with the town of Blairmore, where last year at about this time the Old Man river overflowed its banks and the town was flooded. A number of the streets were practically washed away; several bridges were destroyed to the value I think of $44,000; several of the houses in the town itself had to be moved back from the bank of the river to escape being carried away; the cribbing along the bank of the river for a distance of 2,200 feet was completely washed out; and altogether the town was severely damaged. That town is not financially able to cope with what I think I might term in this case a disaster. If another flood had occurred this year as bad as that of last year there is no doubt in my mind that a considerable portion of the town would have been swept away. The council of the municipality at Blairmore appealed to this government for assistance a year ago, but up to date the department has not seen fit to grant any money to assist in repairing the damage that has been done. The department did send an engineer to Blairmore and he submitted a very complete report of the situation. I am sure that the minister himself is very anxious to give what assistance he can; at any rate he must certainly realize the necessity of granting some money for the erection of the necessary works in the town. His engineer reported that the cost of the dredging and the cribbing which would be necessary to control the river would total $74,100. I want to ask the committee whether they think that a little town with a population of 2,500 could possibly be expected to bear that cost? The Western Canadian Collieries, whose works are located there, have offered to do the work for approximately $50,000. This company operates large coal mines in the town, which is practically dependent on the operation of the mines. The property of the company has been badly damaged by the flood and for that reason they are willing and anxious to co-operate with the municipality towards the construction of the necessary works so that they will not suffer again in the same manner. I want to point out to the committee, and particularly to bring to the attention of the minister, the fact that this government has collected in coal royalties from this company alone the sum of $46S,400 in addition to lease rentals to an amount of $33,300, and for coal lands purchased by the company to the extent of $128,300. This makes a total of $630,000 which has been paid by this one company at Blairmore. Besides this, the government has received from other companies operating in that district the - sum of $796,000, or a total of $1,426,699 received directly from the operators of coal mines in the district. I believe that the town of Blairmore and the property owners affected are quite willing to provide a percentage of the cost of constructing the necessary works, but they are unable to shoulder the entire expense. It is for that reason that I am appealing to the committee and particularly to the minister to bring down an amount in the Supplementary Estimates to take care of part of the cost of erecting the protection works along the banks of the Old Man river through the town of

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Blairmore. I should like to have an assurance from the minister that this will be done.

I would hesitate
to give such an assurance. I have contended that in regard to the condition in the town of Blairmore there is some responsibility on the provincial government, who do collect certain revenues from the community and who therefore should interest themselves, along with the municipality, in getting things straightened out. If that were done I would then be more confident in coming to parliament to ask for a vote for this necessary work-for I believe it is necessary. The Old Man river, as has been said, is a mountain stream and in the spring season it very often becomes a torrent at this point and is very difficult of control, so thalt the people of the town are exposed to periodical floods. This condition however is not peculiar to that section alone. Indeed, rivers all over the world get beyond control at times and cause great damage. We are trying to take care of the situation as best we can, dealing with each case as it comes before us.

I wish to support the minister and the bon. member (Mr. Coote) in the statement that taking care of flooded areas, repairing the dykes on the rivers, and matters of that nature, is a joint responsibility which should be shared by the municipalities and the provinces along with the Dominion. Last year the minister will remember a delegation from Portage la Prairie Waited upon this government and requested either the straightening of the Assiniboine river or the repairing of the dykes in order to meet the situation that develops in that district every feiw years as a result of floods. I stated before that delegation at that time- and my position in this matter
4 p.m. is well known-that in my opinion the province together with the municipality of Cartier and adjoining muncipalities through which the river runs should be prepared to come to the government with a concrete proposal and be willing to assume a certain proportion of the cost required to give the river its proper course. The difficulty, I think, was that we were not in a position to submit any plan of joint action. Fortunately there has been no flood this year, and that explains why the demand upon the government has not been renewed. No doubt, however, the question will come up again in the future; the settlers living in that vicinity are in constant fear of these floods, and the matter is bound to arise 
again. The Dominion government will therefore have to recognize -the necessity for some work being done in connection with this river. If the municipalities directly interested had to put up some money along with the province they would be more careful -about expenditures; there is no doubt about that. Another phase -of the situation in connection with the river seems to be this, that there does not appear to be any one who is right on the job With dynamite to break up the ice jams as they occur and so to prevent flooding. It has happened that in the case of an ice jam occurring on the river, before notification could come from Ottawa to the dynamiting crews the damage had been done, the baulks had -been overflowed and the dykes Washed away. If the municipality had to take its share of the financing it is quite possible that the municipal council would be on the job to repair any damage that might occur. I am not saying they do not do that already, but there is a possibility of their looking to Ottawa to take care of the situation whereas prompt local action might prevent a disastrous flood. Last year $6,000 was provided in the estimates for taking a survey on the Assiniboine river. That survey has been made and I understand the government have a plan in mind for the reclaiming of that great area which is now endangered by periodical floods. No revenue will come to Canada more quickly than that which will result from the reclamation of these valuable lands. The government is getting no income taxes from that portion of Manitoba, now that is largely owing to the floods that have taken place within the last few years. I think it is the duty of this government, the provincial government and the municipalities to join hands with a view to taking care of the drainage situation in that splendid portion of Manitoba.

Just one further word in
connection with the work at Blairmore. The town of Blairmore has been hard hit by the Home Bank disaster. The deposits of the people of that town in the Home Bank amounted approximately to $200,000, and the loans which the bank had there, were $6,000, that is $190,000 more of deposits than of loans. Twenty-five per cent of that has been returned, but the people of the town are still short that seventy-five per cent. The school district of Blairmore, which is part of the town machinery, lost, I think, $10,000 i-n that bank failure. The town has been finding it hard to finance its necessary operations since the Home Bank went under, and that makes it alt

the more important that assistance should be given at this time. There is one fact I did not mention which might further impress the minister with the necessity of giving assistance to the town in this case. The river runs all the way through the town, following a winding course in several places and making necessary a lot of bridges. In this flood the bridges which were washed out were estimated by the engineers of this government to cost $41,000. These bridges have to be repaired or replaced, in addition to the works that I have already mentioned. It seems to me that the people of the town are very reasonable in asking the government to put up possibly fifty per cent of the cost of the construction of these works. I may point out that the same condition exists at Okotoks. It would seem that the property owners first affected might be the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; if that is the case I presume they are quite able to take care of themselves. But it is quite possible that considerable damage might result to the owners of property m that town if the river should change its course even to a very slight degree. I trust that the minister will see that some appropriation is made under which he could, if necessary, give the town of Okotoks some assistance should they suffer from flood next spring. I would again urge upon the minister the necessity of doing something at the town of Blairmore.

Are we to understand that
the government is responsible for damage done by freshets and floods where bridges are taken away or land destroyed, and that kind of thing? If so, there will be a lot of requirements in Ontario along the same line.

No, I do not
think we are responsible in such cases.
I admit I did not know until the discussion came up that the Dominion government was responsible in such cases. However, if they are I want to present a claim of the constituency in which I live.

Not yet.

These prairie rivers are a
little different from rivers in other parts of the country. They run through flat alluvial
plains. The banks are just a little higher at the river than further back and a flood of a few inches will inundate the country for quite a distance back from the river. It will be seen, therefore, that a very small embankment will do a great deal of good. As for the Dominion government paying part of the expense, that is a question for them to decide. In regard to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Leader) as to the Dominion government and the municipalities undertaking this sort of work, I do think, knowing the conditions, that the Dominion government have some responsibility in the matter. But the proper method would be for the municipalities to do the work something after the fashion of drainage districts. The reclamation of a large section would be carried on; the land reclaimed would be owned by several individuals, and the expenses could be charged up against the land benefited. It would not be a question of public charity or of public assistance; a great deal of useful work would be done and the people themselves would be benefited.

I hope nothing I have said
will precipitate a run on the Department of Public Works for assistance to prevent the erosion of banks of streams. But, for the enlightenment of some members, I may point out that in the last ten years, according to a return brought down, there has been spent on harbours and rivers and dredging in Alberta and Saskatchewan the enormous sum of $204,000, while in the rest of Canada there has been spent $82,390,775. Alberta and Saskatchewan have approximately fifteen per cent of the population of Canada, but the amount spent under these heads in those two provinces has been less than one-quarter of one per cent of the amount spent in other parts of the country.

I will admit the force
of what the hon. member (Mr. Coote) has just said, but possibly it has not occurred to him that what 'is railway transportation to the prairie provinces is water transportation with us. In Nova Scotia, for instance, there is one main line of railway running through the centre of the province-not a very well constructed railway, and one which does not give a very excellent service, though it is true that it has been better in the last few years. Practically the whole of the traffic is carried on through these harbours and over the wharves around the shores. I have suggested that when the estimates for harbours and rivers for the Maritime provinces come up we might have a map hung up somewhere

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
in the chamber, if the Speaker would permit it, which would show the location of the harbours and rivers and also the location of the railways in those provinces. I am not finding fault with western members, because I know they do not realize our situation as we do ourselves, and I am willing to admit that we do not realize their situation. But if you compare the amount spent on harbours and rivers in the prairie provinces with the amount spent in the Maritimes, and if you compare also the amounts spent on railroads, I believe you will find they are about the same per capita. To take either alone would not give a fair idea of our methods of transportation or of our necessities along that line.

I should like to point out one feature-I do not know just what there is in it-the provinces other than the three prairie provinces own their own natural resources, and that may make some difference in the obligation the Dominion government has towards them. We would like to have these resources, but we have not got them, and the other provinces have.

If the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) feels he has a grievance because he has not harbours in his district, I would be very happy to let him have a couple of hundred from my district, with the consequent expenditure involved, and there would still be enough left to bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to the grave getting the government to do justice to what was left.

I would point out to the hon-member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) that the prairie provinces, while they do not own their natural resources, get a cash subsidy in lieu thereof every year. It may be that the prairie provinces would prefer their natural resources. We are not arguing that at the moment, but I just wanted to point out to the hon. member that when that arrangement was made the prairie provinces were granted a yearly subsidy in lieu of their natural resources.

Has the coal mining
business been injured by the overflowing of this river at Blairmore?
I have no knowledge of that, but I think not.
If it has been why do the people there wish to build on the bank of a river that is likely to overflow and destroy their property? Is there not room for them to build back from the river?

I might point out to the hon. member that this town of Blairmore is not on the prairie, but in the Crowsnest pass, a pass running through the Rocky mountains. The valley is very narrow, and the only place where they can build the town is in between the two ranges of mountains. The Crowsnest river comes down through that pass. The works owned by the mine, which are on the flat, were very badly damaged, to the extent of a good many thousands of dollars, and the coal mining company has to take care of that damage itself. They are anxious to assist in the work of straightening the river and erecting cribs on each side, backed with rocks, to hold the river from overflowing again and damaging their works. They have a large iron works there, one of the largest, the manager told me, between Winnipeg and Vancouver. They have also sidings leading to their mines. They have a great many buildings on the flat, at the mouth of the mine. These were all in danger, and some of them were damaged. Several bridges were also washed away. This is why the mining company is anxious to co-operate with the government and the town in cribbing the banks of the river to prevent such a thing happening again in the future
I might further explain that the banks of this river in places are not more than four feet high, so when a freshet comes down there is not room in the channel for the water to get away, and last year it spread out all over the flat and flooded practically the whole town. As I pointed out, the Dominion government is receiving a splendid revenue from that little town, and I think it is not asking very much when we ask that the government should meet the wishes of the town of Blairmore in that matter. If I have not explained the situation fully to the satisfaction of the hon. member and the committee, I shall be very glad to do so. I look upon this flood at Blairmore last year in the nature of a calamity which visited that community. The same is true of High River. These are the only two harbours I have in my constituency at the present time. I hope I shall not be looked upon as making undue demands upon the government, but if any member here was to go back home to spend the week-end, and find the town had been flooded three feet deep, and all the bridges had been washed away, and the houses

threatened with the same fate, I am sure he would regard it as a calamity, and it is in that light I am asking this government to regard that flood.

I do not wish to prolong the debate, but I would point out to the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes), who mentioned that the western provinces were receiving a subsidy in lieu of their natural resources, that it is not contended by anybody, I think, that that relieves the Dominion government in any way. The Dominion government grants a subsidy in order to hold those natural resources, and we feel that, possessing them, they are more responsible than they would be otherwise.

What is the vote for, then?

For improvements to navigation. It is for the construction of an extension to the existing north jetty which will direct the current of the stream, and, we hope, will maintain the channel. The expenditure made during the last two years has met with a considerable amount of success. The work is under contract and will be proceeded with.

Is it intended to proceed with this work gradually so that eventually the different points further up the river, Port Mann for instance, will be accessible to deep water boats in future, and will the development made proceed as part of the harbour improvements?

The intention of
the department is to proceed from one stage to the other. The Fraser river near its mouth becomes a very large river, and the spring freshets bring down a tremendous quantity of alluvial and other material which is deposited, oftentimes causing the river to change its course. These jetties are built to control and direct the current in certain channels. We find that very good results have been obtained by the construction of the jetty. A jetty was constructed last year near a place known as the King Edward cut. That work has been closely watched. It is the intention of the department, where the experience of the surveys and examination and watching of currents will show that the construction of these jetties will tend to bring about a correction and make navigable the channel, to put in these jetties rather than to continue the old practice of dredging from year to year. From the engineering point 201* . (
of view I think the work is progressing satisfactorily. It is being carefully watched by the departmental staff.

My interest in this
matter is due to the fact that I looked into that river to some extent while I was in that district during last winter. It is not often a prairie man is very much interested in the rivers and harbours, but I was particularly interested in this point of view: That in my opinion Port Mann on the Fraser river will eventually be the logical shipping point of the Canadian National Railways. The importance of that point can hardly be overestimated, and I certainly hope, as far as practicable, the work will be continued, and that the Canadian National, whose terminus is Port Mann, will be able to utilize the river in their operations.

In common with the
hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) I am greatly interested in this matter; and in confirmation of what was said I call attention to the fact that the shipping on the Fraser river has very greatly increased in recent years. During the last year quite a large number of sea-going vessels have come into the river, largely for the purpose of taking out lumber and other products which are manufactured on the Fraser river. The minister has said that the work is proceeding satisfactorily, but I think possibly that statement is going a little far. I do say, however, that the minister and his department are entitled to credit for the work which has been done. They are showing an intelligent interest in the Fraser river, but at the same time I do not think that the people in New Westminster and vicinity are altogether satisfied with conditions at the present time. They do not think the work has been taken up in a satisfactory way. They do not think the department is energetic enough in this respect, and that it is meeting conditions as readily and as speedily as it should. I am quite aware that the minister has studied the Fraser river, and that his chief engineer has also made a very complete study of conditions there. I understand it is the intention of the minister to go out to the Pacific coast during the coming summer, and I think request has been made that he visit the Fraser river again and also that he if possible take his chief engineer out there again. Mr. Cameron is familiar with the location, and I hope the minister will find it convenient to take him to that district. Conditions are not absolutely satisfactory at the present time. The draught of vessels coming into the port is in-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
creasing, as the minister knows. At the present time ships drawing 25 feet of water are making regular trips. I think the}' are carrying ore for the Canadian Pacific or for some subsidiary company of that company and regular shipments are being made. Those vessels are drawing 25 feet of water, and it is absolutely necessary that the channel be at all times kept in such a condition that these vessels can navigate without difficulty, I know that the board of trade, the city council and other public bodies of New Westminster have made representations to the minister that certain work which they consider absolutely urgent at thlis time should be let by contract. The minister has all these facts before him and I suppose is giving the matter consideration, but I know that he thinks that the people of New Westminster are unnecessarily alarmed. He thinks they are exaggerating the difficulties which they think they have there. I can assure the minister that this is not so. These men are all interested in the future, not only of that district, but of Canada. The busi-nes that we do in New Westminster is export and if it is lost to us it is lost to Canada, f am sorry to have to say that at the present time the two dredges which are supposed to be working on the Fraser river have been taken away. I think this is a great mistake, and I have from time to time impressed upon the minister the necessity of keeping the dredges on the Fraser river until we get the channel into such a shape that it will be permanent. The necessity exists at present, and the matter is not in an experimental stage. The business is there and waiting, and it is very necessary that we should be able to accommodate even deeper draught vessels than are navigating there at the present time. The minister knows that some of the Canadian Merchant Marine vessels are of greater draught than can be accommodated in the channel at the present time. Those vessels would like to go in the Fraser river.
Then we have the matter of the shipment d grain. I have taken occasion from time o time to draw the attention of the minister o facilities which the port of New Westminster presents for the shipment of grain. We have asked the government to establish a grain elevator on the Fraser river. That demand has been made on a great many occasions and has been repeated from time to time. The first time I spoke to the present minister in regard to the matter he said, ''The government does not propose to build any more elevators." The next thing I heard was that they were buying the Woodward

elevator, another elevator in Vancouver. I do not say that I object to that. The announcement was made a few days ago that the government propose to build an elevator at Prince Rupert. I am not objecting to that Put I say that the claims of the Fraser river are such that this government should be particularly interested in them inasmuch as New Westminster or Port Mann is the logical point for the shipment of the grain which goes over the Canadian National Railways. As the minister knows, that is assuming very considerable proportions. At the present time great quantities are coming through New Westminster and are taken over to Burrard Inlet. There is no reason why that grain should be taken to Burrard Inlet at all, because the Fraser river is the first point where the ships can come in where grain can be loaded. If is simply throwing away money to take that grain over to Burrard Inlet. The minister must have the facts before him The delegation, referred to by the last speaker, of Progressive members who came to New Westminster last, winter, are familiar with the facts. They at that time intimated -and I think they confirm me in the statement now-that they are interested, not so much in any particular point or port on the Pacific, but in having their grain handled where it can be handled most cheaply. That is to say, they would like to see their grain handled economically. It may be, as someone has said, that it does not really make any difference to the, shipper whether his grain goes to Burrard Inlet or to the Fraser river, because the rates will be the same to the shipper; but as a matter of fact, lif extra expense is involved in taking that grain over to Burrard Inlet, somebody has to pay for that. ' I am informed that there is an unnecessary expenditure of one cent a bushel in taking that grain over to Burrard Inlet and the trade will eventually have to stand that loss. That is what Progressive members are interested in.
There are other considerations. As the minister knows, the port of Vancouver at the present time is rather congested, and it is difficult for them to handle all the grain that may be expected to go through Pacific ports. I understand this last year the shipments will amount to something like 50,000,000 bushels. I am informed by Progressive members who were at New Westminster last year that within a very few yeans at least 200,000,000 bushels of grain will go through those ports. When that time comes, the extra expense will mean something, and more

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
than that, the congestion will, of course, be much more marked than it is at present.
As the last speaker has mentioned, Port Mann is a very desirable place to ship grain from and Port Mann is the freight terminus of the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National Railways at the present time have in Port Mann ideal sites for the construction of grain elevators, so that no expense would be involved in purchasing sites.
Another feature is in regard to the initial cost of construction. On fresh water the cost of construction of an elevator is very much leas than on salt water. On salt water it is necessary to have concrete construction, and particularly in the port of Vancouver that construction and the necessary excavation which has to be done are very expensive, so that outside of the initial cost of the site, which is very large, of course, at Burrard Inlet because sites there are expensive, the cost of construction of elevators is very much less on the Fraser river than on Burrard Inlet. Not so long ago a prominent elevator engineer, Mr. Howe, who is well known to the minister and also, no doubt, to many members of the committee, reported in favouir of the location of elevators on the Fraser river as against Burrard Inlet. These facts must be taken into consideration, and I think the government are not treating the Fraser river very fairly as regards establishing elevators there.
I am quite satisfied the minister thinks that elevators should be established on the Fraser river and that he is doing what he can to assist in having elevators owned by private companies located there. When the government are going into the business of constructing elevators, they should construct elevators where the grain can be, handled1 in the most economical and cheapest manner. That is what Progressive members are interested in. It comes down to a matter of business, of dollars and cents, and although the cost is absorbed by railroads, the traffic has to bear the unnecessary money that is thrown away in locating elevators on the Pacific coast elsewhere than at New Westminster or on the Fraser river. The minister knows these facts as well as I do, and I have no doubt that if he expressed his personal opinion, he would tell this committee that grain elevators should be located on the Fraser river. Perhaps I have got away from this particular appropriation, and I crave the indulgence of the committee for having done so, but it seems to me that New Westminster and the Fraser river are entitled to a fair deal and I am afraid they are not getting it.
I should like again to impress upon the minister the necessity for keeping the dredges which the department already has on the Fraser river until the work is completed and put into permanent condition, so that the channel there will be assured. If dredging work has to be done in other places-and no doubt there are places where such work has to be done-why not utilise some of the other dredges which the department has out there and which are at present laid up? My idea is that it would pay the department to do a good deal of the work by contract and get the thing finished. This is going to cost money: money is being spent, and I am not altogether satisfied with the results that are being obtained. I believe the business interests in New Westminster are behind me when I impress upon the minister the necessity of considering the advisability of doing more of this work by contract.

My hon. friend
failed to tell the committee that within the last three or four years the channel of the Fraser river has been improved from a depth of 26 feet to a depth of 29 feet. That is a gradual process, and it is well known amongst hydraulic engineers that if you are dealing with rivers of that character, the type of engineering that should be adopted is to build works that will have the rivers cure themselves, and that is the type of engineering which we have adopted on the Fraser river. Building these walls, we find that the current of the river in question is increased and in a little while you have done what my hon. friend would have done next year by dredging. The difference is this, that the river having cured itself through the assistance that you have given it, in all probability you have established what may become a permanent or natural channel, whereas if you were to vote two, three, four or more million dollars-because it would take that much to dredge a channel from the mouth of the Fraser to New Westminster sufficiently deep to allow boats such as we hope to get, to enter the river, probably the thing would be destroyed the next season. So that so far as we are concerned, and in the interests of the people of Westminster, it seems to me that, it would be better to have a little patience now and allow the men who are studying conditions on the spot to move as they think best. We are hoping that if my hon. friend will be patient, with the scientific knowledge that we are trying to bring to bear upon the problem, if we are allowed to advance from stage to stage we shall accomplish something that will be of

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
real importance and of permanency in the channel. I am not coming to parliament asking for large sums of money in order that we may rush in and dig channels which probably will be closed up a year afterwards; I think the better plan is to proceed scientifically with the problem. This problem is a difficult one which has been studied by the department for many years, and as minister of the department I am going to take the best advice I can get. Nothing pleases me more than to have a conference with the hon. member, with the boards of trade interested, and with the people of the district who are anxious to have the work go on. But it is necessary that we should take a fair view of this as of other matters. I believe that if we follow the plan suggested by our experts we shall accomplish something which will be of permanent use and of abiding satisfaction to the people of Westminster. The activities during the last few years have brought about marked results, results that are very satisfactory to the department. Last year witnessed the largest tonnage that ever went through the river, and very little difficulty was experienced, steamers going in and out easily.

The minister is absolutely right when he says that the proper thing to do is to keep the water of the Fraser river within the channel and let it cut its own way out to the gulf. I remember in 1909 there was a great deal of dredging done on the north arm of the river; in fact, that year there was spent I think about $100,000 on this work. There is one

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I can throw some light on this very vexed question. First let me say that from Ottawa eastward for almost one hundred and twenty-five miles there is no bridge over the Ottawa river. At the capital there are the interprovincial bridges. Towards their construction the provinces and the Dominion contributed one-third each. That would be a precedent apparently, but that precedent was not carried out at first in connection with the Hawkes-bury bridge. An agreement was entered into for its construction just prior to the war, but owing to the outbreak of hostilities operations on the bridge were discontinued. At. that time the government of Quebec were under an agreement to make a grant of $15,000 towards the construction. In the particular locality there is a stretch of the river which for almost fourteen miles is very turbulent owing to the rapid fall of the stream. For that reason no ferries can operate and it is almost impossible for the people in the locality to cross the river. A very serious mistake was made in not making provision for pedestrian and vehicular traffic when the Canadian National Railway bridge was built across the river at that point. However, that was not done, and it seems to me when such difficulties exist along both sides of the Ottawa river for such a long distance, that at this point provision should be made for traffic across the river. The people of the locality have been agitating the matter with both the provincial governments and the federal authorities, and the minister has intimated to the other governments concerned that he is
willing to make a contribution on the same basis as in the case of the interprovincia! bridges at Ottawa, namely, that there should be a split three ways. I know from observation that the structure is very badly needed. As it will be of an interprovincial character, as the precedent to which I have referred exists, and as the federal government prior to the war assumed the responsibility of starting the construction with a very small grant from the provinces, it seems to me that our present action is only an evidence of good faith. That is the situation, and that is the reason this item appears in the estimates. It is for the purpose of commencing construction if an agreement can be reached with the provincial governments.

I do not want to be in the position either of opposing or supporting this particular project. I really want to get at the principle which underlies it. Am I to understand that this is put forward by a member of the government as a general principle that will be applicable to similar conditions elsewhere? Further I should like to know if this bridge will connect two lines of highway which run for a considerable distance from the river, and not merely link up two communities on the river that are practically opposite one another. I will wait for a moment.

Then I want to warn the

They can run for a day if the weather is all right and the water is smooth, but the water there sometimes gets rough very rapidly, and many a time after having gone for only a few hours, they have had to beach the boat and caulk it. The hull is so rotten that the friction of the water and the waves grinds the caulking out, and in some cases after only two hours running they have been compelled to beach her. Suppose they were where they could not beach her at the end of the two hours? Some time that boat will literally and absolutely fall apart. This has already been fully represented to the government, and for my part I am not prepared to take any responsibility beyond that. I have given the exact facts of the case. go out in this boat in its rotten condition- you may say they are not compelled, but they are compelled to if they want to get a living-one of these days there will be a catastrophe.

Perhaps it is not strictly in order on this vote, Mr. Chairman, but as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has spoken about a boat I would like to call the attention of the minister to the Tyrian, a cable boat operating in the Maritime provinces. I am not particularly concerned with the boat itself, although it is a very old boat, and a very great deal of money has been spent on her, but I would like to ask the minister if there is any provision for superannuation and retiring allowances for the men who are operating on the Tyrian and other cable boats. It seems to me most peculiar that the Marine and Fisheries should retire masters from the lighthouse tenders and from their other boats, under the Calder Act and other retiring acts, while the crew of the Tyrian receive no consideration in that respect. That is what I understand from Captain Peters, who happens to be a personal friend of mine, although not a political friend, I think; at all events, he has not a vote in my constituency. He is a first-class seaman and a friend of mine, though a much older man than I am. He was a personal friend of my. father's, and I have known him since I was a boy. Speaking with him last summer he drew to my attention the fact that while the Marine and Fisheries department retire their men on other ooats under the Calder Act and other regulations providing for an allowance, the officers and crew of the Tyrian, which is a very much larger boat than many of the boats owned by the Marine and Fisheries department, are thrown to the four winds of heaven, so to speak, when they are too old to go to sea. These men who are repairing the government cables or any other cables have a very important duty to perform. They have to go around the roughest portion of the shores of the country where these cables are laid by the federal government, around the northern shores of Cape Breton, for instance, the island of Grand Manan, the northern portions of New Brunswick, and around the shores of Prince Edward Island, and any person who has ever gone to sea knows that these men have to brave great dangers in order to carry on their work. It has often seemed to me that the officials of the department at Ottawa 203
particularly in regard to marine matters and the hardships that are endured by the sailors working for the department, are absolute landlubbers and absolutely incompetent to rightly apprehend the dangers these men have to undergo. I am absolutely in accord with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni when he calls to the attention of the minister the condition of the boat he mentioned in British Columbia. I do not know anything in particular about that boat, but I know this, that the officials at Ottawa are too prone to ask these sailors, who are some of the best people in the Dominion of Canada, to endure great risks simply because landlubbers are not prepared to give them the proper equipment they need to carry on their work. I happened to be an official of the Marine and Fisheries department in days gone by, and I found in that department an absolute ignorance, with the exception of two or three of the officials, as to the conditions under which our sailors and fishermen have to work. I believe that the time has come when everything pertaining to the sea should be dealt	with by men who are
thoroughly qualified and who know and can appreciate what these men have to undergo.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear". I wonder if he means that sarcastically. I want to tell him that the men who navigate ships and whose forefathers navigated ships on the seven seas, and who could navigate any ship, from the ordinary schooner to a full-rigged ship, in every quarter of the globe, and carried the flag of Canada to the ends of the earth, and built up a maritime trade for this country, are men of superior intelligence and courage to the man who grows a few grains of wheat on the western prairie, and I say in all seriousness that the time has come in this country when we should get down to practical facts and not be so much concerned whether we grow wheat and provide proper transportation facilities and have the Crowsnest pass agreement. We want something done for the men of the Maritimes, and when I use that term I mean the three provinces on the Atlantic coast. We also want something done for the sailors on the Pacific coast, because all these men are made of as good stock as the individuals who are engaged in any other walk of life.
Shall the item pass?

Is it possible to

I have given some thought to that. The ordinary public works engineer is not considered to be an architectural man. I admit some men who have had good all-round experience could undertake maintenance of buildings; but generally

Supply-Public Works

I have been making some inquiries and one can look at the public accounts. I will read Hansard to-morrow.

Supply-Public Works

As I have
pointed out, the apparent salary list for this department is $631,520 whereas the real amount is $3,752,311.
Would not part of that relate to work done by day labour?

Some of it but not very much. There is however, a tremendous amount of it that ought to be given in this civil government list. Now I ask the hon. member what reason there was for not doing it. He gave me the same reason as was given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have expressed my views upon that kind of an argument, and I asked him if there was not some real reason, and he said yes there was-I am giving what he said just as well as I can recall it-and the real reason was that if all these were put on the civil government list we would be making a whole lot permanent who ought to remain temporary. I pointed out to the Acting Minister of Finance that that is no reason at all, as he well knows. It may be the Minister of Public Works thought it was a reason, but the Acting Minister of Finance knows perfectly well, in his position, that when you are treating everything as Ottawa you have permanent employees as well as temporary employees. Just because they are in Ottawa does not make them permanent, and conversely in connection with outside employees you have permanent and temporary; they are not made temporary because they are outside. It is ludicrous, simply ludicrous. There is no reason advanced by the minister why this reform should not be instituted, and I am going to ask my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance if he knows of any, and if he will not admit that it is infinitely better, when you are looking for salaries, to know where you will find them, whether it is salaries in Ottawa or anywhere else.

I am impressed with the observations of my hon. friend, and to-morrow I shall direct the attention of the department to them, and see if we cannot work out a system next year that will be a little more illuminating.

Perhaps my
hon. friend thinks he has not rushed enough through yet. I just want to point out that this is Friday night, that members who are usually interested in the estimates go away on Friday night, and that the House rises at eleven. That has been the usual rule. I draw the minister's attention to the fact that it is now 11.30.

Notwithstanding the rule referred to the estimates have got through very nicely and conveniently to-night. I am merely pointing out the fact.

speechtext:
I also point
out the fact that when I made the suggestion I did at an earlier period of the sitting it was conditional on its acceptance by my hon. friend and his colleagues. He had only to say that it was not acceptable and the committee would have risen.

Before you leave the
chair, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say I am somewhat surprised at the attitude of the exMinister of Finance because I can remember sitting here when his government brought down new estimates at this time of night and went on until two or three o'clock in the morning.
Not on a Friday night.

I do not know as to
that. But just there I do not see any reason why those of us who have to be here for five months and do not get home at all should be compelled to cease doing business because someone else wants to go home. The members who live near Ottawa have just as much right to be present on Friday night and Monday afternoon as we have. I object to the attitude assumed by the ex-Finance Minister and I do not think he is very serious in his view.

I do not know that I am very serious one way or the other but I like consistency some time. I know what the Prime Minister and the Hon. Mr. Fielding have said about sitting until eleven o'dock. I know all that, but I suppose I should not look for consistency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government has tried to carry on the business so as to conclude our sitting at eleven o'clock, but now that we are getting near the end of the session I think there is a general wish on the part of the House that we should sit somewhat later. Of course, if there is going to be strong objection to sitting late, as far as the government is concerned we will not do so but will continue the session on into July and August if that is preferable. However we want to meet the wishes of members, and I think the general desire is to get through as early as possible.

If the government want to expedite the session let them expedite their measures and bring them down. If they are sincere in wanting to get away they will at least bring down their supplementary estimates. Usually before there is any talk about rushing business and closing the session all the business is brought down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not want to take up very much time but my hon. friend knows better than to speak as he does with respect to the business of the House. If he refers to the records when he was Minister of Finance he will find that the supplementary estimates were not tabled until the last day or the last two days of the session.
' Sir HENRY DRAYTON: The main supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say the main supplementary estimates, I said the supplementary estimates.
Main supplementaries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, supplementary estimates. We gave the House plenty of time to discuss the supplementary estimates. There will be no effort to crowd anything through. With respect to the business of the House there has not been a day when the House has not had all the business before it that it could possibly get through with.

I do not know about that. We have adjourned very early sometimes.
